title: Definition
body_md:
A $U^p(a,b)$ atom is a step function
\[
a(t)=\sum_{k=1}^K \mathds{1}_{[t_{k-1},t_{k})}(t) \phi_k , \quad \sum_{k=1}^K\|\phi_k\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)}^p=1,
\]
$U^p(a,b)$ is the atomic space based on these atoms, that is $u \in U^p(a,b)$ if
\[
u = \sum_{j \in \mathbb{N}} \lambda_j a_j,
\]
where $(\lambda_j) \in l^1$ and $a_j$ are atoms as above; $U^p(a,b)$ is equipped with the standard norm
\[
\|u\|_{U^p(a,b)} = \inf \{ \sum_{j \in \mathbb{N}}  |\lambda_j |:  u = \sum_{j \in \mathbb{N}} \lambda_j a_j \ \mbox{as above} \}. 
\]

title: Definition
body_md:
Given a function $v: (a,b) \rightarrow L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ we define
\[
|v|_{V^p} =\sup_{\tau=\{(t_j)_{j=1,N}\}} \left( \sum_j \| v(t_{j+1}) -v(t_j) \|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)}^p \right)^\frac1p, 
\quad  \|v\|_{V^p} = |v|_{V^p} + \|v\|_{L^\infty_t L^2_x}. 
\]
We let $V^p=V^p(a,b)$ is the space of functions  $v: (a,b) \rightarrow L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ for which $ \|v\|_{V^p}$ is finite.

title: Remark
body_md: In practice, the distributions $f$ that we test will have additional properties such as $f \in L^1_{t, loc} L^2_x$, and, as a consequence, the associated $u$ with the property $f = \partial_t u$ comes with a priori continuity properties $u \in C_t L^2_x$. In order to uniquely identify $u$, either in $U^p$ or $V^p$, one has to impose a normalization, such as the standard one in $U^p$, $\lim_{t \rightarrow a+} u(t)=0$, or the standard one in $V^p$, $\lim_{t \rightarrow b-} u(t)=0$.

title: Remark
body_md: In practice, the distributions $f$ that we test will have additional properties such as $f \in L^1_{t, loc} L^2_x$, and, as a consequence, the associated $u$ with the property $f = (i\partial_t -\Delta) u$ comes with a priori continuity properties $u \in C_t L^2_x$. In order to uniquely identify $u$, one has to impose a normalization, such as the standard one in $U^p_\Delta$, $\lim_{t \rightarrow a+} u(t)=0$, or the standard one in $V^p_\Delta$, $\lim_{t \rightarrow b-} u(t)=0$, or the one imposed by the initial data $u(t_0)=u_0$.

title: Proof
body_md:
To keep the exposition compact, assume $N(z)=z^2$; it is easy to adapt the argument below for the general case $N(z)=c_1 z^2 + c_2 \bar z^2$.

For fixed $z_0 \in \dot H^{-\frac12}$, we define the operator $T: \dot X^{-\frac12} \rightarrow \dot X^{-\frac12}$ as the solution of the equation
\[
(i \partial_t - \Delta) Tz= z^2, \quad z(0)=z_0.
\]
Below we establish  that $T: \dot X^{-\frac12} \rightarrow \dot X^{-\frac12}$ is a contraction. 
The first step is a qualitative observation. A direct estimate shows that
\[
\| P_{k_3} ( P_{k_1} z \cdot P_{k_2} z) \|_{L^\infty_t L^2_x} \lesssim \|P_{k_1} z\|_{L^\infty_t L^\infty_x} 
\| P_{k_2} z\|_{L^\infty_t L^2_x} \lesssim 2^{\frac{nk_1}2} \|P_{k_1} z\|_{V^2_\Delta} \|P_{k_2} z\|_{V^2_\Delta}.
\]
This guarantees that $P_{k_3} ( P_{k_1} z \cdot P_{k_2} z) \in L^1_{t,loc} L^2_x$, hence  $P_{k_3} T ( P_{k_1} z, P_{k_2} z) \in C_t L^2_x$, in particular it is a ruled function; this also provides the qualitative estimate $P_{k_3} T ( P_{k_1} z, P_{k_2} z) \in C_t \dot H^{-\frac12}$, which can then be recovered globally using the uniform estimates described below. 

From \eqref{mtri} and \eqref{mtri2} we obtain the following bound
\[
2^{-\frac{k_3}2} \| P_{k_3} T ( P_{k_1} z, P_{k_2} z) \|_{V^2_\Delta} \lesssim 2^{(\frac12 - \epsilon)(k_{min}-k_{max})} 2^{-\frac{k_1}2}  \|P_{k_1} z \|_{V^2_\Delta} 2^{-\frac{k_2}2} \|P_{k_2} z \|_{V^2_\Delta}. 
\]
A direct summation argument shows that $T$ is bounded on $\dot X^{-\frac12}$. Moreover, we also obtain the contraction type bound
\[
\| Tz_1 - Tz_2 \|_{\dot X^{-\frac12}} \lesssim (\| z_1 \|_{\dot X^{-\frac12}} + \| z_2 \|_{\dot X^{-\frac12}}) \| z_1-z_2 \|_{\dot X^{-\frac12}}. 
\]
Therefore, under the assumption that the initial data $\|z_0\|_{\dot H^{-\frac12}}$ is small enough, $T$ becomes a contraction in $\dot X^s$, which in turns leads to the existence of a fixed point $z$ which corresponds to a global solution of the equation \eqref{QNLS}. Scattering is a consequence of the fact that functions in $V^2_\Delta$ have well-defined limits as $t \rightarrow \pm \infty$. 

The rest of the claims in Theorem \ref{thm gwp} are standard and follow from similar arguments.

label: eq:anisotropic-kernel
title: Proof
body_md:
The case $p=\infty$ follows from the anisotropic Bernstein bound
  \[
    \|e^{-it\Delta}f\|_{L_t^\infty L_x^q}
    \lesssim
    |S|^{\frac12-\frac1q}\|f\|_{L_x^2}
    \lesssim
    2^{2k(1-\frac2q)}\|f\|_{L_x^2}.
  \]
  We may therefore assume that $p<\infty$. For simplicity, we assume that $S$
  is centered at $e_1$. We let $Af= e^{-it\Delta}\chi (D) f$,
  where $\chi$ is a smooth cutoff to a slightly enlarged copy of $S$.
  The operator $AA^*$ is a spacetime convolution operator with kernel
  \[
    K_k(t,x)
    =
    \int_{\mathbb R^3}
      e^{i(x\cdot\xi+t|\xi|^2)}
      \chi(\xi)^2\,d\xi.
  \]
  By the $TT^*$ argument, it suffices to prove
  \[
    \|AA^*\|_{L_t^{p'}L_x^{q'}\to L_t^pL_x^q}
    \lesssim 2^{(2k+j) \left(1-\frac{2}{q}\right) - \frac{4k}{p}}.
  \]
  For this we use the pointwise kernel bound
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:anisotropic-kernel}
    |K_k(t,x)|
    \lesssim
    2^{2k+j}(1+2^{2k}|t|)^{-1}.
  \end{equation}
  Interpolating the resulting $L_x^1\to L_x^\infty$ estimate with the
  $L_x^2\to L_x^2$ bound and then using Young's inequality in $x$, we
  obtain
  \[
    \|K_k(t,\cdot)*_x\phi\|_{L_x^q}
    \lesssim    2^{(2k+j)(1-\frac2q)}
    (1+2^{2k}|t|)^{-(1-\frac2q)}
    \|\phi\|_{L_x^{q'}}.
  \]
  If $\frac1p+\frac1q=\frac12$, then
  $1-\frac2q=\frac2p$, and the Hardy--Littlewood--Sobolev inequality in
  the time variable gives
  \[
    \|AA^*F\|_{L_t^pL_x^q}
    \lesssim
    2^{(2k+j)\left(1-\frac{2}{q}\right)} (2^{-2k})^{\frac2p}
    \|F\|_{L_t^{p'}L_x^{q'}}.
  \]
  If $\frac1p+\frac1q<\frac12$, the same conclusion follows from
  Young's inequality in the time variable, since
  $1-\frac2q>\frac2p$. This proves the required $AA^*$ bound.

  It remains to prove \eqref{eq:anisotropic-kernel}. Write
  \[
    \xi_1=1+2^{2k}\rho,
    \qquad
    \xi'=2^k\eta,
    \qquad
    \xi'=(\xi_2,\xi_3).
  \]
  After removing a phase of absolute value one, we obtain
  \[
    K_k(t,x)
    =
    2^{4k}
    \int_{\mathbb R}
      e^{i(2^{2k}(x_1+2t)\rho+2^{4k}t\rho^2)}
      \int_{\mathbb R^2}
        e^{i(2^kx'\cdot\eta+2^{2k}t|\eta|^2)}
        a(\rho,\eta)\,d\eta\,d\rho,
  \]
  where $a$ is smooth, supported in a fixed bounded set, and has uniform
  symbol bounds. 
  By stationary phase in the variable $ \eta $,
  \[
    \left|
      \int_{\mathbb R^2}
        e^{i(y\cdot\eta+s|\eta|^2)}
        a(\rho,\eta)\,d\eta
    \right|
    \lesssim
    (1+|s|)^{-1},
  \]
  uniformly in $\rho$ and $y$. Taking $s=2^{2k}t$ and
  $y=2^kx'$, and estimating the remaining $\rho$-integral directly,
  yields \eqref{eq:anisotropic-kernel}.

  The transference to $ U_{ \Delta }^{ 4 } $ follows immediately for atoms: if
  $ a(t) = \sum_{ J }  \1_{ J }e^{ -it\Delta } \phi_{ J }   $ is a $ U_{ \Delta
  }^{ 4 } $-atom,
  \begin{align*}
    \lVert a \rVert _{ L_{ t,x }^{ 4 }  } ^{ 4 }
    &\lesssim \sum_{ J } \int_{ J }\lVert e^{ -it\Delta } \phi_{ J }  \rVert _{
    L_{ t,x }^{ 4 } }^{ 4 }
    \lesssim 2^{ j } \sum_{ J } \lVert \phi_{ J }  \rVert_{ L_{ t,x }^{ 4 }
    }^{ 4 },
  \end{align*} 
  since the time intervals $ J $ are disjoint.
  The estimate for generic $ U_{ \Delta }^{ 4 } $ functions then follows by
  density.
